items.title: Q1 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The deductive method differs from the inductive method in drawing its conclusions from
items.explanation: In logic and research methodology, the deductive method reasons from general truths, axioms, or established premises down to specific conclusions. Conversely, the inductive method observes particular empirical instances in order to formulate general laws or theories.

items.title: Q2 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which one of the following journals publishes articles related to critical theory exclusively?
items.explanation: Founded in 1971 at Cornell University and published by Johns Hopkins University Press, Diacritics: A Review of Contemporary Criticism is an academic journal devoted exclusively to critical theory. Callaloo focuses on African diaspora arts and letters, while Salmagundi and Grand Street are broader cultural and literary quarterlies.

items.title: Q3 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Which one of the following assumptions best expresses the position of Post-Structuralist
criticism?
options: Apprehension of reality is a construct
Knowledge operates according to procedures that are axiomatic
items.explanation: Post-structuralist criticism rejects the idea that language transparently represents a fixed external world or rests on stable, axiomatic structures. Instead, it argues that human apprehension of reality is a linguistic and discursive construct shaped by shifting play of signifiers.

items.title: Q4 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which one of the following is correct about Saussure's analysis of language?
options: La langue is the system of a language
Parole focuses on language as a system at a particular time
La langue is the particular instance of speech and writing
Parole is the study of language over a period of time
items.explanation: In Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (1916), la langue refers to the abstract, shared system of rules and conventions that constitutes a language. It contrasts with parole, which denotes concrete, individual instances of speech or writing.

items.title: Q5 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Who among the following theorists particularly emphasized the social and historical
dimensions of a text's reception?
items.explanation: German literary theorist Hans Robert Jauss (a key figure of the Constance School alongside Wolfgang Iser) emphasized the social and historical dimensions of a text's reception in Toward an Aesthetic of Reception (1982). Jauss introduced the 'horizon of expectations' to show how readers in different historical periods interpret a literary work.

items.title: Q6 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · George Herbert
items.stem: Which one among the following is a set of the Metaphysical Poets?
options: John Dryden, George Herbert, and Alexander Pope
Henry Vaughan, John Dryden, and John Donne
John Donne, Henry Vaughan, and Andrew Marvell
Samuel Johnson, T.S. Eliot and Herbert Grierson
items.explanation: John Donne, Henry Vaughan, and Andrew Marvell (along with George Herbert, Richard Crashaw, and Abraham Cowley) belong to the seventeenth-century Metaphysical Poets. Characterized by intellectual wit, dramatic directness, and elaborate 'metaphysical conceits', they were grouped together by Samuel Johnson in his 'Life of Cowley' (1779).

items.title: Q7 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Aristotle
items.stem: Which one of the following statements is true about Aristotle's poetics?
options: He asserted the value of poetry by integrating rhetoric and imitation (mimesis)
He asserted the value of poetry by focusing on both rhetoric and imitation (mimesis)
He asserted the value of poetry by giving preference to rhetoric over imitation (mimesis)
He asserted the value of poetry by focusing on imitation (mimesis) rather than rhetoric
items.explanation: In his treatise Poetics, Aristotle defines poetry and drama fundamentally as modes of imitation (mimesis) that represent human action and universal truths, whereas he treats persuasive speech separately in his Rhetoric. By grounding poetry in mimesis and catharsis, Aristotle defended its philosophical and moral value against Plato's critique.

items.title: Q8 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:
Who said of the blank verse, quoting an unnamed critic, that it is "...verse only to the eye",
adding further that it "has neither the easiness of prose, nor the melody of numbers"?
items.explanation: At the close of his 'Life of Milton' in Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1779–1781), Samuel Johnson critiques English blank verse as lacking the distinct musicality of rhyme. Quoting 'an ingenious critic' (William Mason), Johnson remarks that blank verse seems to be 'verse only to the eye' and 'has neither the easiness of prose, nor the melody of numbers'.

items.title: Q9 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Poetry according to Sir Philip Sidney is of three kinds. They are
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (The Defence of Poesie, 1595), Sir Philip Sidney classifies poetry into three kinds: religious (divine poetry that imitates the inconceivable excellencies of God, such as the Psalms), philosophical (didactic verse teaching moral, natural, or historical knowledge), and imaginative ('right poets' who imitate to teach and delight).

items.title: Q10 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In Anxiety of Influence which of the following definitions is given by Harold Bloom to explain
the term, 'clinamen'?
items.explanation: In The Anxiety of Influence (1973), Harold Bloom outlines six 'revisionary ratios' by which belated poets wrestle with their strong precursors. The first ratio, clinamen (borrowed from Lucretius's swerve of atoms), is defined by Bloom as 'poetic misreading or misprision proper', whereby a poet swerves away from a precursor's text.

items.title: Q11 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who among the following is known to have popularized the term 'glocalization'?
items.explanation: British sociologist Roland Robertson popularized the concept of 'glocalization' (adapted from the Japanese business term dochakuka) in his book Globalization: Social Theory and Global Culture (1992) and his 1995 essay 'Glocalization: Time-Space and Homogeneity-Heterogeneity', describing the simultaneous interpenetration of global and local cultures.

items.title: Q12 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who among the following coined the dictum, "the medium is the message"?
items.explanation: Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan coined the famous aphorism 'the medium is the message' in Chapter 1 of Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man (1964). McLuhan argued that the formal characteristics of a communication medium shape human association and perception far more profoundly than the specific content it carries.

items.title: Q13 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem:
Who among the following presented the concept of 'multi-accentuality' of the sign, saying
that signs possess an 'inner dialectical quality' and 'evaluative accent'?
items.explanation: In Marxism and the Philosophy of Language (1929), Soviet linguist Valentin Voloshinov (associated with the Bakhtin Circle) introduced the 'multi-accentuality' of the ideological sign. Voloshinov argued that because different social classes use the same language, every sign becomes an arena of class struggle possessing an 'inner dialectical quality' and 'evaluative accent'.

items.title: Q14 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
On December 11, 1823, Rammohan Roy addressed a letter to the British authority which
pleaded for modern western education and is considered historically important for the
introduction of English education in India. Who was the letter addressed to?
items.explanation: On 11 December 1823, social reformer Raja Rammohan Roy addressed a historic letter to Lord Amherst, the Governor-General of India. Protesting the British government's plan to establish a Sanskrit College in Calcutta, Roy pleaded instead for modern Western instruction in mathematics, natural philosophy, chemistry, and anatomy.

items.title: Q15 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Sir Thomas Munro, Lord Cornwallis
items.stem: Which British administrator sought "to make everything as English as possible in a country which resembles England in nothing", as recorded by Sir Thomas Munro?
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Munro, Governor of Madras, criticized Lord Cornwallis's administrative and judicial reforms (including the Permanent Settlement of Bengal in 1793), observing that Cornwallis's system sought 'to make everything as English as possible in a country which resembles England in nothing.' Munro advocated instead for the ryotwari system that accommodated existing indigenous traditions.

items.title: Q16 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following was the first Director of the Central Institute of English and Foreign
Languages, Hyderabad (now EFL University)?
items.explanation: Kannada writer and English scholar Prof. Vinayak Krishna Gokak (V. K. Gokak) served as the founding Director of the Central Institute of English (later CIEFL, and now the English and Foreign Languages University) when it was established in Hyderabad in 1958.

items.title: Q17 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which one of the following best explains the term 'paralanguage'?
options: The ways in which people mask what they mean by the words they use
The ways in which people show what they mean other than by the words they use
The ways in which words carry meanings unintended by the speaker
The ways in which the silence underlying speech communicates wrong meanings
items.explanation: In linguistics and communication studies, paralanguage (coined by George L. Trager in 1958) refers to the non-lexical vocal and non-verbal features—such as pitch, volume, intonation, tempo, sighs, and facial expressions—through which speakers convey meaning and attitude beyond the literal words they utter.

items.title: Q18 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following oppositions are best evoked by Hamlet's utterance - "To be or not
to be"?

A. between life and death

B. between action and emotion

C. between affirmation and confirmation

D. between doing and abstaining from doing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In Act III, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's Hamlet, Prince Hamlet's soliloquy 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' weighs two fundamental oppositions: the existential choice between life and death (continuing to live versus ending one's life), and the moral dilemma between active resistance ('taking arms') and passive endurance ('abstaining from doing').

items.title: Q19 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Who among the following linguists proposed the terms, 'competence' and 'performance'?
items.explanation: American linguist Noam Chomsky introduced the distinction between linguistic 'competence' and 'performance' in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965). Competence denotes an ideal speaker-listener's innate, unconscious knowledge of grammatical rules, whereas performance refers to the actual production and comprehension of language in concrete situations.

items.title: Q20 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which one of these statements defines the scope of semiotics?
options: Semiotics studies the sound systems of a language
Semiotics is a study of sign systems
Semiotics studies human sign system only
Semiotics is a study of non-human sign systems only
items.explanation: Semiotics (from Greek sēmeion, 'sign') is the general study of signs, sign systems, and processes of signification across both human culture and the natural world. Developed independently by American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce and Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (who called it semiology), it examines how meaning is produced and interpreted.

items.title: Q21 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Thomas Hobbes
items.stem:
Which according to Thomas Hobbes is the only 'science' God has bestowed on mankind, that
informs the structure of his monumental work, Leviathan?
items.explanation: In Chapter 4 ('Of Speech') of Leviathan (1651), Thomas Hobbes declares that Geometry is 'the only science that it hath pleased God hitherto to bestow on mankind'. Admiring Euclid's deductive method of reasoning from clear definitions to indisputable conclusions, Hobbes modelled his political philosophy on geometrical demonstration.

items.title: Q22 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · William Hazlitt
items.stem:
As mentioned in "My First Acquaintance with Poets" which poet does William Hazlitt describe
as the "only person | ever knew who answered the idea of a man of genius"?
items.explanation: In his autobiographical essay 'My First Acquaintance with Poets' (published in The Liberal in 1823), William Hazlitt recalls hearing Samuel Taylor Coleridge preach at Shrewsbury in January 1798. Hazlitt praises Coleridge's spellbinding eloquence, calling him 'the only person I ever knew who answered to the idea of a man of genius'.

items.title: Q23 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Virginia Woolf
items.stem: Which one of the following essays holds that "As a method, realism is a complete failure"?
options: Virginia Woolf, "The Mark on the Wall
items.explanation: In his Socratic dialogue essay 'The Decay of Lying' (1889, collected in Intentions, 1891), Oscar Wilde's mouthpiece Vivian champions Aestheticism over nineteenth-century naturalism. Vivian declares that 'As a method, realism is a complete failure', arguing instead that Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life.

items.title: Q24 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following novels is structured into a poem of 999 lines, preceded by a
Foreword, followed by a Commentary and an Index?
options: The Inner Side of the Wind
items.explanation: Vladimir Nabokov's metafictional novel Pale Fire (1962) is presented as a 999-line autobiographical poem in heroic couplets by fictional American poet John Shade, accompanied by a Foreword, lengthy line-by-line Commentary, and Index written by his delusional neighbour and self-appointed editor, Charles Kinbote.

items.title: Q25 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Donald Barthelme
items.stem:
Which among the following novels includes a questionnaire for the reader such as "Do you like
the story so far? Yes() No()"?
options: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller by Italo Calvino
items.explanation: Donald Barthelme's postmodern novel Snow White (1967) concludes Part One with a satirical fifteen-question survey directly addressing the reader, beginning with '1. Do you like the story so far? Yes ( ) No ( )' and asking whether the novel has enough emotion or should be abandoned.

items.title: Q26 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What is the subject of Ivan's controversial essay in Brothers Karamazov?
items.explanation: In Book II, Chapter 5 ('So Be It! So Be It!') of Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880), the intellectual sceptic Ivan Karamazov discusses his controversial newspaper article on the jurisdiction of ecclesiastical courts, arguing that the State should eventually be absorbed completely into the Church.

items.title: Q27 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Which one of the following Sherlock Holmes stories refers to a significant event in English history?
items.explanation: In Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes short story 'The Musgrove Ritual' (The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, 1893), Holmes deciphers an enigmatic 17th-century ritual preserved by the Musgrove family. It leads to the discovery of the battered ancient royal crown of King Charles I, hidden away during the English Civil War and forgotten after the Restoration of Charles II.

items.title: Q28 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Harold Skimpole is a character in
items.explanation: Harold Skimpole is a character in Charles Dickens's novel Bleak House (1852–1853). Modelled caricaturally on essayist Leigh Hunt, Skimpole is a charming but thoroughly selfish parasite who claims to be a 'mere child' in matters of money and responsibility while living off the generosity of John Jarndyce.

items.title: Q29 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Mary Shelley
items.stem: Who is the author of "A Fragment" (1819), one of the earliest vampire stories in English?
items.explanation: Lord Byron composed the unfinished prose tale 'A Fragment' (centering on the mysterious aristocrat Augustus Darvell dying in the ruins of Ephesus) during the famous ghost-story contest at the Villa Diodati in June 1816. Byron published it alongside Mazeppa in 1819, and his physician John Polidori expanded its premise into The Vampyre (1819).

items.title: Q30 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Kamala Markandaya
items.stem: Lala Kanshi Ram is a character in
options: Anita Desai's Fire on the Mountain
Kamala Markandaya's A Handful of Rice
items.explanation: Lala Kanshi Ram is the central protagonist of Chaman Nahal's Sahitya Akademi Award-winning Partition novel Azadi (1975). A prosperous Hindu grain merchant in Sialkot, Kanshi Ram is uprooted with his family by the communal violence of the 1947 Partition and forced to migrate as a refugee to Delhi.

items.title: Q31 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin
items.stem: Which of the following poems by Philip Larkin deals with the trauma of a rape victim who says "Even so distant, I can taste the grief"?
items.explanation: Philip Larkin's poem 'Deceptions' (from The Less Deceived, 1955) takes its epigraph from Henry Mayhew's London Labour and the London Poor regarding a girl drugged and ruined. The poem begins: 'Even so distant, I can taste the grief, / Bitter and sharp with sighs, / For your conduct was shameful...'

items.title: Q32 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Seamus Heaney
items.stem: In which of the Bog poems does Seamus Heaney speak about the "perishable treasure" of a body "Murdered, forgotten, nameless, terrible"?
items.explanation: In Seamus Heaney's sonnet 'Strange Fruit' (from his 1975 collection North), Heaney describes the exhumed head of an ancient bog girl: 'Here is the girl's head like an exhumed gourd... / Let the perishable treasure of her face / Murdered, forgotten, nameless, terrible / Beheaded girl, outstaring axe / And beatification...'

items.title: Q33 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem:
Which book of Paradise Lost incorporates the speech rhythms of Adam and Eve's marital
quarrel?
items.explanation: Book 9 of John Milton's Paradise Lost dramatizes the temptation and Fall of humankind. It opens with a domestic disagreement between Adam and Eve over working separately in Eden, and concludes with their bitter marital quarrel and mutual recriminations after eating the forbidden fruit.

items.title: Q34 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · William Cowper
items.stem:
Who among the following wrote Mazeppa, a long narrative poem about a seventeenth-century
military leader of Ukraine?
items.explanation: Lord Byron wrote the Romantic narrative poem Mazeppa (published in 1819), inspired by Voltaire's History of Charles XII. In the poem, the aged Ukrainian Cossack Hetman Ivan Mazepa recounts to King Charles XII of Sweden how, as a young Polish court page punished for an affair, he was bound naked to the back of a wild horse.

items.title: Q35 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem: Which one of the following statements is appropriately true of Harold Pinter's plays?
options: Menace is in the air and it leads to bloody violence
Menace is in the air and it is realized through the female characters
Menace is in the air, but it is not pinned down, or explained
Menace is in the air and anarchy follows in a systematic manner
items.explanation: Early plays by Harold Pinter—such as The Room (1957), The Birthday Party (1958), and The Dumb Waiter (1959)—were termed 'Comedies of Menace' by critic Irving Wardle. In Pinter's dramatic world, a pervasive,nameless dread and threat of intrusion hang in the air, yet the exact source or motive of the menace is never explicitly explained.

items.title: Q36 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: To which mythological character is Faustus compared in the Prologue of Dr. Faustus?
items.explanation: In the Prologue of Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), the Chorus compares Faustus's intellectual hubris in turning from theology to necromancy to the mythological figure of Icarus: 'His waxen wings did mount above his reach, / And melting heavens conspired his overthrow.'

items.title: Q37 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
Who makes the following speech in Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot?

"Astride of a grave and a difficult birth. Down in the hole, lingeringly, the grave-digger puts on
the forceps."
items.explanation: Vladimir speaks these famous lines in Act II of Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) while Estragon sleeps onstage. Echoing Pozzo's earlier lament ('They give birth astride of a grave'), Vladimir reflects on the brevity and absurdity of human existence, where birth and death merge into a single moment.

items.title: Q38 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit I: Drama · William Congreve
items.stem: Which of the following are the major themes in William Congreve's The Way of the World?
items.explanation: William Congreve's Restoration comedy of manners The Way of the World (1700) revolves around the themes of love, financial calculation, and social intrigue. Its labyrinthine plot follows the witty lovers Mirabell and Millamant as they outmanoeuvre Fainall, Mrs. Marwood, and Lady Wishfort to secure both marriage and Millamant's inheritance.

items.title: Q39 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem: What game do the characters play in Act Il of Harold Pinter's The Birthday Party?
items.explanation: In Act II of Harold Pinter's The Birthday Party (1958), Lulu suggests playing a game of blind man's buff during the sinister party held for Stanley Webber. When it is Stanley's turn to be blindfolded, McCann deliberately breaks Stanley's spectacles and places the toy drum in his path, precipitating his psychological breakdown.

items.title: Q40 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · John Webster
items.stem: The Duchess of Malfi is based on
items.explanation: John Webster's Jacobean revenge tragedy The Duchess of Malfi (c. 1613, published 1623) is ultimately based on an Italian novella by Matteo Bandello (loosely recounting the historical marriage of Giovanna d'Aragona, Duchess of Amalfi, to her steward Antonio Bologna), which Webster read in William Painter's English translation in The Palace of Pleasure (1567).

items.title: Q41 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Which two of the following strictly follow the parameters of documentation prescribed by the
eighth edition of the MLA Handbook?

A. Nunberg, Geoffrey, editor. The Future of the Book. U of California P, 1996.

B. Puig, Manuel. Kiss of the Spider Woman. Trans. Thomas Colchie, London: Vintage, 1991.

C. Nunberg, Geoffrey, ed. The Future of the Book. Berkeley: U of California P, 1996.

D. Puig, Manuel. Kiss of the Spider Woman. Translated by Thomas Colchie, Vintage Books, 1991.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The eighth edition of the MLA Handbook (2016) streamlined bibliographic citations by eliminating the city of publication and replacing traditional Latinate abbreviations like 'ed.' and 'Trans.' with spelled-out roles ('editor' and 'Translated by'). Entries A and D strictly follow these eighth-edition rules, whereas B and C use older seventh-edition conventions.

items.title: Q42 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
A research hypothesis is :

A. a proposition which is always true

B. a provisional explanation of anything

C. a theory which will be disproved by evidence

D. a statement which is assumed to be true for the sake of argument
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In research methodology, a hypothesis is a tentative, provisional explanation of a phenomenon (B) or a testable proposition assumed to be true for the sake of investigation and argument (D). It is neither an indisputable axiom that is always true nor a theory guaranteed in advance to be disproved.

items.title: Q43 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Which two of the following aspects are to be scrupulously followed to avoid the trap of
plagiarism?

A. subjectivity

B. acknowledgement

C. citation

D. interpretation

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Plagiarism is the uncredited appropriation of another person's words, ideas, or research findings. To avoid plagiarism in scholarly writing, researchers must scrupulously practice proper acknowledgement (crediting intellectual debts) and accurate citation (providing in-text references and bibliographic entries).

items.title: Q44 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jamaica Kincaid
items.stem:
Which two texts among the following are linked to literary feminism?
A.A Small Place

B. The Yellow Wallpaper

Cc. Emma

D. A Room of One's Own

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's short story 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (1892), which critiques the patriarchal 'rest cure' imposed on women, and Virginia Woolf's foundational feminist essay A Room of One's Own (1929), which argues that a woman needs financial independence and private space to write fiction, are landmark texts of literary feminism. A Small Place (1988) by Jamaica Kincaid is a postcolonial critique of tourism in Antigua.

items.title: Q45 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following feminist theorists posited a separate realm of female experience
captured in a style of writing different from men's?

A. Elaine Showalter

B. Luce Irigaray

C. Kate Millett

D. Simone de Beauvoir

E. Helene Cixous

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: French feminist theorists Hélène Cixous (in 'The Laugh of the Medusa', 1975) and Luce Irigaray (in Speculum of the Other Woman, 1974, and This Sex Which Is Not One, 1977) advanced the concept of écriture féminine and parler-femme—a distinct mode of female writing rooted in the female body and pre-Oedipal experience that subverts phallocentric language.

items.title: Q46 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem:
Which of these statements describe correctly the basic assumption of Structuralism?

A. Structuralism is concerned with signs and signification.

B. A structuralist theory considers only verbal conventions and codes.

C. Structuralism began in the works of Jacques Derrida that influenced the 20th-

century literary criticism.

D, Structuralism challenges the long-standing belief that literature reflects a given reality.
E. All signs are arbitrary but without them we cannot comprehend reality.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Grounded in Ferdinand de Saussure's semiology, Structuralism is concerned with signs and signification (A), challenges the mimetic assumption that literature merely mirrors a pre-existing reality (D), and holds that although linguistic signs are arbitrary, we cannot structure or comprehend reality without them (E). Statement B is false because structuralism also analyzes non-verbal cultural codes, and Statement C is false because Jacques Derrida inaugurated Post-Structuralism.

items.title: Q47 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two terms among the following are associated with formalist criticism?
A. aura

B. actant

C, narratee

D. defamiliarization

E. foregrounding

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: 'Defamiliarization' (ostranenie), coined by Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky in 'Art as Technique' (1917), and 'foregrounding' (aktualisace), developed by Prague School theorist Jan Mukařovský, are core concepts of formalist criticism that explain how poetic language disrupts habitual perception. By contrast, 'aura' belongs to Walter Benjamin, while 'actant' (Greimas) and 'narratee' (Prince/Genette) belong to structuralist narratology.

items.title: Q48 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth, Philip Sidney, Horace
items.stem:
Who among the following believed that rhyme is not an integral part of poetry?
A. William Wordsworth

B. Horace

C. Samuel Daniel

D. Philip Sidney

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Classical Roman poet Horace (in Ars Poetica, written in unrhymed hexameters) and Renaissance critic Sir Philip Sidney (who stated in An Apology for Poetry that 'it is not rhyming and versing that maketh a poet') both maintained that rhyme is merely an ornament rather than the defining essence of poetry. By contrast, Samuel Daniel defended rhyme in A Defence of Ryme (1603).

items.title: Q49 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton, John Dryden
items.stem:
Who among the following are the two great masters of the French language that T. S Eliot
contrasts with Dryden and Milton in "The Metaphysical Poets"?
A. Francois Villon

B. Jean Racine

C. Charles Baudelaire

D. Arthur Rimbaud

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In his 1921 essay 'The Metaphysical Poets', T. S. Eliot argues that while John Milton and John Dryden triumphed with a 'dazzling disregard of the soul', French literature avoided this dissociation of sensibility. Eliot writes: 'The two greatest masters of diction are also the greatest two masters of the heart: Racine and Baudelaire.'

items.title: Q50 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Which two terms from among the following are specifically linked to the work of Pierre
Bourdieu?

A. habitus

B. consciousness

C. desire

D. distinction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu developed the concepts of 'habitus' (ingrained, socially acquired dispositions of thought, taste, and bodily deportment) and 'distinction' (how aesthetic tastes and cultural capital mark social class hierarchies) in Outline of a Theory of Practice (1972) and Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste (1979).

items.title: Q51 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Macaulay's Minute of 1835 sought to :

A. promote European literature and science among the natives.

B. impart knowledge of English literature and science through translated texts.
C. encourage branches of native learning by more useful studies.

D, stop expenditure on the publication of oriental works and spend funds only on English
education.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (2 February 1835) resolved the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy by urging the colonial government to promote European literature and science among Indians through the medium of English (A), and to halt official expenditure on printing Arabic and Sanskrit Oriental texts (D).

items.title: Q52 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following statements are applicable to 'metalanguage'?

Itis:

A. a technical language which describes the properties of language.

B. known as a 'first-order' language.

C. a 'second-order' language that replaces a 'first-order' language with metaphors.
D. a 'second-order' language.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In logic, linguistics, and semiotics (notably in Alfred Tarski, Roman Jakobson, and Roland Barthes), a 'metalanguage' is a technical or analytical language used to describe and analyze the properties of an ordinary 'object language' (A). Because it operates upon a first-order object language, it is defined as a 'second-order' language (D).

items.title: Q53 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)

about the above sentence?

B. The sentence is an example of structural ambiguity.

C. The sentence involves two deep structures.

D. The sentence involves two surface structures.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In transformational-generative grammar, the sentence 'Hari wrote a poem on the mountains' (meaning either that Hari was on the mountains while writing, or that the poem's topic was the mountains) exhibits structural (syntactic) ambiguity (B). A single surface structure here corresponds to two distinct underlying deep structures (C).

items.title: Q54 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following events are described in Samuels Pepys's Diary?
A. The Plague in London

B. The Great Fire of London

C. The War of Spanish Succession

D, Essex Rebellion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Kept in shorthand from 1660 to 1669, Samuel Pepys's Diary provides vivid first-hand eyewitness accounts of Restoration London, most famously the Great Plague of London (1665) and the Great Fire of London (September 1666). The Essex Rebellion occurred earlier in 1601, and the War of the Spanish Succession took place later from 1701 to 1714.

items.title: Q55 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Which two of the following inspired the rise of the periodical essay?
A. Robert Burton

B. Francois Rabelais

C. Francis Bacon

D, Michel de Montaigne

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: French Renaissance humanist Michel de Montaigne, who coined the genre in Essais (1580), and English philosopher Francis Bacon, who adapted the form into pithy English prose in Essays (1597–1625), were the two primary models who inspired eighteenth-century periodical essayists such as Joseph Addison and Richard Steele.

items.title: Q56 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman · Unit I: Drama · Walter Pater, Dante Alighieri
items.stem:
Which two of the following works does Walter Pater regard as examples of "great art" in his
essay "Style"?

A. Iliad

B. The Divine Comedy

C. Les Miserables

D. Faust

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: At the close of his 1888 essay 'Style' (collected in Appreciations, 1889), Walter Pater distinguishes between 'good art' (formal perfection of expression) and 'great art' (which is dedicated to the noble enlargement of human sympathy and truth). Pater explicitly names Dante's The Divine Comedy, Milton's Paradise Lost, Victor Hugo's Les Misérables, and the English Bible as examples of 'great art'.

items.title: Q57 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Henry David Thoreau
items.stem:
According to his essay "Civil Disobedience", what two things did Thoreau learn from the night
he spent in jail?

A. He concluded that the State is ultimately weak.

B. He realized that captivity inspires courage.

C. He realized that the neighbours are only friends during good times.

D. He concluded that captivity brings wisdom about human affairs.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In 'Civil Disobedience' (1849), Henry David Thoreau reflects on his night in Concord jail for refusing to pay the poll tax. He concludes that the State is ultimately weak and 'half-witted' because it can only lock up his physical body (A), and realizes upon his release that his townsmen are merely fair-weather friends unwilling to risk comfort for justice (C).

items.title: Q58 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)

Mail - Coach"?

A. The Glory of Mobility

B. The Vision of Sudden Death

C. The Glory of Motion

D. The Vision of Unexpected Truth

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Thomas De Quincey's 1849 essay 'The English Mail-Coach' is divided into three celebrated sections: Section I, 'The Glory of Motion' (celebrating the exhilarating speed of the royal mail-coach system); Section II, 'The Vision of Sudden Death' (recounting a terrifying near-collision at night); and Section III, 'Dream-Fugue'.

items.title: Q59 · Oct 2020 (Set 2)

Which two of the following books are explorations of the art of the novel by novelists?
A. The Brief Compass

B. The Naive and the Sentimental Novelist

C. The Visionary Company

D. Testaments Betrayed

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The Naive and the Sentimental Novelist (2010, Charles Eliot Norton Lectures) by Turkish Nobel laureate Orhan Pamuk and Testaments Betrayed (1993) by Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera are both book-length explorations of the art of the novel written by practising novelists. By contrast, The Visionary Company (1961) is a study of English Romantic poetry by critic Harold Bloom, and The Brief Compass (1985) is a scholarly study of the German novella by Roger Paulin.

B. Marlowe

D. Keats

items.explanation: British novelist Anthony Burgess wrote biographical novels about several English writers, including Christopher Marlowe in A Dead Man in Deptford (1993), John Keats in ABBA ABBA (1977, depicting Keats's final months in Rome), and William Shakespeare in Nothing Like the Sun (1964).

Which two rivers are mentioned by Andrew Marvell at the beginning of "To His Coy Mistress"?

B. Thames

C. Humber

D. The Jhelum

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In the opening verse paragraph of Andrew Marvell's metaphysical carpe diem poem 'To His Coy Mistress' (published 1681), the speaker tells his beloved that if they had infinite time, 'Thou by the Indian Ganges' side / Shouldst rubies find; I by the tide / Of Humber would complain'—contrasting the exotic Indian Ganges with the river Humber near Marvell's hometown of Hull.

D. Katherine Philips, "A Married State"

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 'Ulysses' (1842), spoken by the aged king of Ithaca, and Carol Ann Duffy's 'Medusa' (from The World's Wife, 1999), spoken by the jealous mythological Gorgon, are both classic dramatic monologues delivered by a distinct persona. Philip Larkin's 'Church Going' (1955) is a meditative lyric, and Katherine Philips's 'A Married State' (1664) is a didactic advice poem.

Logic cannot have any empirical part; that is, a part in which the universal and necessary laws of thought should rest on grounds taken from experience; otherwise it would not be logic, i.e, a canon for the understanding or the reason, valid for all thought, and capable of demonstration. Natural and moral philosophy, on the contrary, can each have their empirical part, since the former has to determine the laws of nature as an object of experience; the latter, the laws of the human will, so far as it is affected by nature: the former, however, being laws according to which everything does happen; the latter, laws according to which everything ought to happen. items.explanation: In the preface to Immanuel Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), Kant explains that formal logic cannot have an empirical part because its universal laws of thought do not rest on sensory experience.
